newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Committee head says CFP reform main fisheries priority.
newsitem.headline: Committee head says CFP reform main fisheries priority.

text.p: The European Union's common fisheries policy is a failure and needs a radical overhaul, the newly chairwoman of the European Parliament's fisheries committee said on Wednesday.
Carmen Fraga Estevez said the aims of the CFP -- to conserve dwindling fish stocks and reduce overcapacity -- were good ones but the system failed to work in practice.
"I think we have to change the CFP radically," the Spanish Conservative Euro-MP told Reuters in an interview.
"It's a failure because it's very complicated to control and no one is actually controlling it."

The member states, who were responsible for preventing overfishing, complained about their neighbours' fleets but failed to contain their own fishermen, who were all involved in a mad scramble for what scarce resources remained, she said.

Fraud could be reduced, she suggested, by giving the European Commission more powers to enforce the rules, not only through new satellite monitoring of fleets' movements but also through road checks on lorries transporting fish.

"It's very important to detect rules on minimum fish sizes are respected," Fraga Estevez said, adding that the Spanish, French and Greek fishing industries were making an effort to comply but were being undermined by Italian imports of illegally small fish.

The former lawyer said it was also vital to overhaul the system of national fishing quotas to reduce illegal fishing and reduce the pressures on those member states which wanted to preserve their fishing industry.
Germany, for example, hardly used its national quota, while Spain wanted more fish, couldn't get it and was having to lay up its boats, she said.
She suggested keeping an overall EU ceiling on catches but letting individual fleets compete for licences, rather than setting national quotas.
This would only be workable, she added, if the industry was properly restructured first and overcapacity reduced.

Fraga Estevez also wants total admissible catches to be set by scientists, not EU fisheries ministers, run for a period of years instead of being changed annually, and cover several species at a time.
The fisheries committee is pushing for a thorough debate with the Commission and the industry on the future of the CFP, expected to take place in late summer.
"I hope we can get a compromise on the future of the sector. It can only work if it's a compromise between the politicians and the sector," Fraga Estevez said.
The Spanish Euro-MP has also made it her job to convince the Council of Ministers that a common fisheries policy is in the interest of all member states.
Most member states believed the CFP only benefited France, Spain and Portugal and complained it was too costly, she said.
They had to realise the benefits went much further, limiting the EU's large deficit in fish products, thus keeping prices to consumers down, and providing jobs in both production and processing.
And the actual cost of the CFP was derisory, equivalent to what the EU spent on subsidising the tobacco industry, she pointed out.

The apparent hostility towards the CFP of member states like Britain and Germany served to undermine the Commission's negotiating position in international fishing agreements, according to Fraga Estevez.

She said the parliament's role in the debate would be more effective if Euro-MPs were allowed to participate as observers in these negotiations, a proposal which fisheries commissioner Emma Bonino has agreed to consider.
Bonino's officials have also agreed to discuss with the committee in two weeks time the Commission's proposals for technical fish stock conservation measures.
Fraga Estevez said she supported the proposal's general lines but insisted there must be a transition phase for their introduction, in order to reduce the social and economic costs they entailed.
Under Fraga Estevez's leadership, the fisheries committee is expected to keep up pressure on the Council to overcome the impasse over proposals to ban all driftnet fishing by the end of 1997.
It also intends to continue blocking a proposal which would waiver rules on the mimimum permitted size of fish for Italian vessels working the Adriatic.
"We shouldn't allow them a derogation to fish legally what was illegal before and discriminate against France, Spain and Greece," Fraga Estvez said.
